turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, have a seat. What has been going on with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I had a hernia operation ten days ago, and the wound has turned rather red.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to jump in. I'm his carer, I stay at the house during the week. The dressing was wet with a yellow stain this morning.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, that is not what you want after an operation. Tell me how the recovery had been going before this.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The first several days were quite acceptable. I was moving about the house, slowly. Then the skin beside the cut began to look angry.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister next door took the plaster off just now, before we came in. She said there is yellow stuff on the gauze, and she left it open for you.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Helpful. Which side was the hernia, and did they do it open or with a camera?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The right groin. It was an open repair, at the day theatre, and I went home the same afternoon. They put a mesh in, or so the surgeon told me.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the redness start? As near as you can.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not entirely sure of the day. Perhaps Saturday, or it may have been Sunday. I cannot put a proper date on it.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I only saw the skin properly on Sunday evening, when I helped him shower. The dressing was still on before that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you feel feverish at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night, yes. I felt very hot, and shivery with it. I did not read the thermometer myself.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ja, I did. It was thirty-eight point nine... no, thirty-eight point four. I misread it the first glance, sorry.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, thirty-eight point four last night. How are you feeling sitting here now?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired, Doctor, and rather washed out. The shivering has stopped. I still feel a little warm, but the fever seems to have settled.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the wound itself painful?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): It is. A burning pain, worse when I walk. If I sit, it eases.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was awake a good part of the night with it. I did give him pain tablets, I'll explain in a moment.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): There was also the matter of the parking. The robot outside was out, and the boom was stuck, and we nearly turned around. I apologise for arriving a little flustered.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): No stress at all. Let me look at the wound. Just lie back a bit.

[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. The cut is in the right groin. The skin around it is red for about the length of my finger, and there is a little yellow discharge at the lower end. The stitches are still in. It feels warm. I am not feeling a pocket of pus underneath.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that a serious infection, Doctor?

[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not going to put a firm label on it this minute. It may be a superficial wound infection, it may be a stitch abscess, and I cannot rule out a small collection a bit deeper. I will not say the mesh is involved, not on today's look. We'll see what the tests say before I go further than that.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister thought it looked infected, but she said you must decide.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. How is your appetite, and have you had any nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): My appetite has been poor since yesterday. I have not vomited. There has been no diarrhoea either.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): And passing urine? Any burning, or going more often?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): That has been entirely normal. No burning, and not more often.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any redness in the other groin, or red streaks down the thigh?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does get a bit short of breath on the stairs. He tells me that was already there before the operation, from not being fit.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park the fitness for another visit. I don't want to chase that today. What medicine did they send you home with?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): An antibiotic, co-amoxiclav. The strength was five hundred... no, six hundred and twenty-five milligrams, three times a day, by mouth. They said it was to prevent infection after the operation.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days did you actually take it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? I finished the packet. I honestly cannot tell you which it was.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box is on the kitchen table at home. I think the label said a week, but I would not swear to that.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you are not taking it now?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Correct. I took the last tablet two or three days ago. I am not on it at present.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about pain relief?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado, the paracetamol, one gram by mouth, up to four times a day, when the pain requires it. Yesterday I also took ibuprofen, two hundred milligrams... forgive me, four hundred milligrams, by mouth, with food, twice.

[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While we are on tablets, his brother uses metformin for his diabetes. The brother was lecturing him about sugar on the phone. He has not taken any of his brother's tablets.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite so. My brother has diabetes. I do not. I did not take a single one of his tablets.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. We'll leave your brother's metformin right out of your notes. Are you on any regular medicine of your own? Blood pressure, anything like that?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Nothing regular, apart from what I have already mentioned.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): How have you been looking after the wound at home?
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We tried to keep it dry. He showered on Sunday and the dressing got damp, so I changed it with gauze from the chemist.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I may also have walked too much. I went to the shops on Friday. Perhaps that provoked it.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking is usually encouraged after this operation, so I would not blame the shops. Let me take your numbers.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temperature now is thirty-seven point six. Pulse is ninety-six. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight. Your oxygen saturation is ninety-eight percent on room air.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Is a pulse of ninety-six a concern?
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is a little fast, which fits with your body dealing with this. Your tummy is soft, and there is no guarding away from the wound.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He only managed tea and one slice of toast this morning. I wasn't sure if I should mention that.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you did. Here is what I would like to do. I will take a wound swab now and send it to the lab. And I would rather change the antibiotic than restart the co-amoxiclav.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): What would you prefer I take, Doctor?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flucloxacillin, five hundred milligrams, by mouth, four times a day, for seven days, for this wound infection. Start this afternoon, if the pharmacy downstairs has stock.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the old ones, should he... oh, he has already finished them. Sorry.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do not restart the co-amoxiclav. The flucloxacillin replaces it. Try to take it on an empty stomach, about an hour before food.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I will be careful with the timing.

[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the Panado as you have been, for the pain. For the ibuprofen, hold it. Actually, leave it off completely until I see you again. I don't want it on an empty stomach while we treat this.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Understood. I will stop the ibuprofen.

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads quickly, or the fever goes above thirty-eight point five again, or you start vomiting, go to casualty. Do not wait for me. Otherwise I want to see you here in two days.
[SEG0063] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days. I'll ask at the desk on the way out.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): And the stitches, Doctor? Should they come out?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave them for now. If the swab, or the look of the wound when you return, suggests we should release a stitch, we can do that then. I am not opening it today.
[SEG0066] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sister asked whether you want a dressing back on.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): A dry dressing is fine. Change it if it becomes soaked. Please don't pack anything into the wound.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): May I ask whether this is likely to spoil the repair?

[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): I do not think so, and I am not concluding that the repair has failed. Most wounds like this settle with antibiotics and simple care. I won't say more until the swab is back.
[SEG0070] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was also fretting about work. He is a bookkeeper, mostly sitting at a desk.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Desk work can start again when you feel up to it. No lifting anything heavier than a kettle until I review you. That is the bit I would stick to.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. That is quite clear.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): The swab goes today, I will write the script, and reception can book the two-day visit. Anything you still want to ask?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. You have been most kind. We shall do exactly as you have said.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch that he takes the new antibiotic properly. Thank you.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pleasure. Look after that wound, and I will see you in two days.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Ibuprofen 400 mg by mouth taken twice yesterday is supported; discontinuation only instructed now, not prior medication status.
bad.text: ibuprofen (dose=400 mg, route=oral, frequency=twice, indication=pain, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: No regular medicines of his own apart from those already mentioned.
Co-amoxiclav course duration is uncertain: patient said 5 or 7 days and finished the packet; caregiver thought the label said a week but was not sure. He took the last tablet 2–3 days ago.
Ibuprofen instruction was stronger than recorded: doctor first said hold it, then clarified to leave it off completely until review because he did not want it on an empty stomach.
Appetite detail from caregiver: this morning he only managed tea and one slice of toast.
Negative finding asked and answered: passing urine was entirely normal.
Examination finding/assessment nuance: doctor was not saying the mesh was involved based on today's look.
Plan detail: doctor was not opening the wound today.
